metadata.description: Properly grounded dataset with verified expected_contexts for precision@K, recall@K, and hit@K evaluation. Each expected_context has been verified to contain relevant information for answering the question.
metadata.verification_method: Each candidate file was read and verified to contain information relevant to answering the specific question. Files that only tangentially mention topics without providing useful context were excluded.

test_cases.question: What are Pods?
test_cases.ground_truth: A Pod is the smallest and simplest Kubernetes object. It represents a set of running containers on your cluster.
test_cases.verification_notes: _index.md contains exact answer; pod-lifecycle.md contains lifecycle details for pods

test_cases.question: How are Kubernetes Secrets stored by default in the API server's underlying data store?
test_cases.ground_truth: By default, Kubernetes Secrets are stored unencrypted in the API server's underlying data store (etcd).
test_cases.verification_notes: secret.md line 36 contains exact answer; secrets-good-practices.md line 28 also mentions unencrypted storage in etcd

test_cases.question: What does the node controller do when a node becomes unresponsive in the Kubernetes cluster?
test_cases.ground_truth: When a node becomes unresponsive, the node controller checks with the cloud provider's API to see if the server has been deactivated, deleted, or terminated. If the node has been deleted from the cloud, the controller deletes the Node object from the Kubernetes cluster.
test_cases.verification_notes: cloud-controller.md lines 52-55 contain exact answer; nodes.md lines 209-225 discuss node controller eviction behavior

test_cases.question: What happens to the nominatedNodeName field of Pod P when a higher priority Pod arrives and is given Node N instead?
test_cases.ground_truth: When a higher priority Pod than Pod P arrives and is given Node N, the scheduler clears the nominatedNodeName of Pod P. By doing this, the scheduler makes Pod P eligible to preempt Pods on another Node.
test_cases.verification_notes: pod-priority-preemption.md lines 198-212 contain detailed explanation of nominatedNodeName clearing behavior

test_cases.question: Can you join a Windows server as a worker node to a Kubernetes cluster?
test_cases.ground_truth: Yes, it is possible to join your Windows server as a worker node to a Kubernetes cluster. According to the text, the CNCF and Linux Foundation take a vendor-neutral approach towards compatibility, which enables this functionality.
test_cases.verification_notes: _index.md lines 15-16 confirm Windows servers can be worker nodes; intro.md lines 38-40 discuss Windows node capabilities

test_cases.question: What formula should you use to determine if your container needs a startup probe instead of relying solely on a liveness probe?
test_cases.ground_truth: According to the text, if your container usually starts in more than `initialDelaySeconds + failureThreshold × periodSeconds`, you should specify a startup probe. This formula helps determine when the standard liveness probe configuration would not allow enough time for container startup.
test_cases.verification_notes: pod-lifecycle.md lines 755-760 contain the exact formula

test_cases.question: What happens to a pod with a NoExecute toleration that specifies tolerationSeconds: 3600 when a matching taint is added to the node it's running on?
test_cases.ground_truth: When a matching NoExecute taint is added to the node, the pod will stay bound to the node for 3600 seconds, and then be evicted. If the taint is removed before that time, the pod will not be evicted.
test_cases.verification_notes: taint-and-toleration.md lines 162-176 show example with exact behavior described

test_cases.question: What parameter is required when configuring a gang policy for a pod group in a Kubernetes Workload?
test_cases.ground_truth: When configuring a gang policy for a pod group in a Kubernetes Workload, the `minCount` parameter is required. This parameter specifies the number of Pods that must be schedulable simultaneously for the group to be admitted.
test_cases.verification_notes: policies.md lines 45-52 show gang policy with minCount; gang-scheduling.md lines 28-32 explain minCount usage

test_cases.question: What happens to the node selection when a CSI storage driver cannot create a volume on the initially selected node for a Pod with WaitForFirstConsumer volumes?
test_cases.ground_truth: When the CSI storage driver cannot create the volume on the initially selected node, the node selection is reset. The Kubernetes scheduler then tries again to find a node for the Pod.
test_cases.verification_notes: storage-capacity.md lines 80-89 describe exact rescheduling behavior when volume creation fails

test_cases.question: What happens to the PersistentVolumeClaim created for a generic ephemeral volume when the Pod that uses it gets deleted?
test_cases.ground_truth: When a Pod that uses a generic ephemeral volume gets deleted, the ephemeral volume controller ensures that the PersistentVolumeClaim gets deleted as well. The controller creates the PersistentVolumeClaim when the Pod is created and automatically deletes it when the Pod is deleted.
test_cases.verification_notes: ephemeral-volumes.md lines 193-218 explain Pod ownership and garbage collection of PVCs

test_cases.question: In what order does Kubernetes evict Pods from a Node when it runs out of resources?
test_cases.ground_truth: When a Node runs out of resources, Kubernetes will first evict BestEffort Pods running on that Node, followed by Burstable and finally Guaranteed Pods.
test_cases.verification_notes: pod-qos.md lines 30-33 give exact eviction order; node-pressure-eviction.md lines 332-339 provide detailed ranking
